item.title: Deterministic Quantum Search for NP Problems Through Verifier-Based Oracle Construction
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — NP search problems solved with unit success probability in O(N/M) oracle queries using verifier-based reversible quantum circuits requiring O(poly(n)) qubits.

Grade 0.416 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Soumyajyoti Chatterjee, Harishankar Mishra, Asvija Balasubramanyam, S D Sudarsan, Gudapati Naresh Raghava

Figure

Measured state probability for a 4-variable 4-SAT instance after 3 calibrated iterations. The single valid assignment 1101 is found with probability exactly 1.0.

Asks

How can quantum search deterministically identify satisfying assignments for general NP problems directly from their classical polynomial-time verifiers without losing the quadratic query speedup?

But

Requires exact prior knowledge of the number of valid solutions M (or the initial success probability); ideal state-vector simulation without noise.

Tools

ancilla-assisted deterministic amplitude amplification · reversible Boolean circuits · Qniverse state-vector simulation

Code. https://github.com/C-DAC-Bengaluru/Qniverse/tree/main/quantum-algorithm-developments/Deterministic%20Quantum%20Search%20for%20NP%20problems

Abstract

Problems in the class NP are important in computational science, where a given candidate solution can be verified in polynomial time, while finding a solution may require evaluating the entire search space in the worst case. Classical exhaustive approaches generally solve such problems by evaluating the verifier function over all possible inputs, resulting in a worst-case query complexity of O(N), where N = d^n represents the size of the search space, d is the number of possible values for each variable, and n is the number of variables. Quantum search algorithms can solve unstructured search problems more efficiently by reducing the query complexity to O(sqrt (N)), providing a quadratic speedup over classical exhaustive search. However, conventional quantum search formulations typically assume access to an oracle that identifies valid solutions, while standard implementations generally yield probabilistic success. In this work, we propose a generalised quantum oracle construction method for NP problems, together with a deterministic quantum search framework that identifies satisfying assignments using their corresponding classical verifier functions. The proposed framework retains the quadratic query speedup of quantum search over classical exhaustive search. We further establish that constructed oracle can be implemented using a number of gates polynomial in the size (L) of the binary encoding of verification function, consistent with the polynomial-time evaluation of the corresponding classical verifier, while the total qubit requirement remains O(poly(L)). The construction is demonstrated on multiple N-SAT instances, with circuit-level simulations confirming deterministic identification of satisfying assignments. These results establish the applicability of deterministic quantum search to NP problems while retaining the quadratic query advantage over classical exhaustive search.

item.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Discovers and formally verifies quantum circuits across 5 benchmarks, lowering logical spacetime volume Q⋅𝒯 up to 290x for arithmetic and 2.5x to 11x for large-scale scientific simulations.

Grade 0.414 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser, Francisco J. H. Heras, Nicholas C. Rubin, Guang Hao Low, Sébastien Racanière, Nenad Tomavsev, Lei M. Zhang, James Watson, Tanuj Khattar, Aws Albarghouthi, Stavan Jain, Harun Khan, Leopoldo Sarra, Andrew W. Senior, Michael Broughton, Hussain Masoom, Sergio Boixo, Ryan Babbush, Swarat Chaudhuri, Pushmeet Kohli

Figure

Resource costs for quantum algorithms across applications comparing prior baselines against verified discovered circuits, showing logical qubit and T-gate reductions.

Asks

Can multi-agent LLM systems automatically discover and formally verify resource-reduced quantum algorithms at scales beyond classical simulation?

Before

For cytochrome P450, prior compiled baseline was Qbase⋅𝒯base=1.09×1012 (Q=481, 𝒯=2.26×109).

But

Circuits and proofs target fault-tolerant architectures counting logical qubits and T gates (Q⋅𝒯); assumes idealized clean ancilla reset and exact/bounded-error synthesis without physical noise models.

Tools

Lean 4 interactive theorem prover · Quantum Hoare logic (QHL) · LLM multi-agent collaborative framework · One-hot Givens rotation synthesis

Abstract

The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

item.title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Amplitude-encoding state preparation simplifies multiplexer circuits to 1- and 2-qubit gates, reducing circuit depth by up to orders of magnitude at equivalent state fidelity compared to standard multiplexer methods.

Grade 0.409 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Vittorio Pagni, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Felderer, Michael Epping, Kevin Lively

Figure

Ratio of CX-depth of the proposed Binary-Tree methods (BT-BE, BT-WHT, BT-Hybrid) to Qiskit's state-preparation circuit depth plotted against qubit count n across various target function families, demonstrating depth reductions of several orders of magnitude.

Asks

How can generic high-dimensional complex data or queryable functions be deterministically loaded into quantum states without exponential memory or circuit-depth overhead?

Before

Möttönen multiplexer-based state preparation decomposed generic states in Θ(N/n) depth via Shende recursive trees (as implemented in Qiskit), requiring dense storage of 2(2n−1) angles.

But

Boolean simplification involves an NP-hard optimization problem; Walsh-Hadamard method requires one clean ancilla qubit; memory reduction to O(2lχ2) relies on low Matrix Product State bond dimension χ.

Tools

Tensor Train / Matrix Product State representation · Tensor Cross Interpolation · Boolean logic Disjoint Sum of Products minimization · Walsh-Hadamard Transform · IQM superconducting quantum processor

Abstract

Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.

item.title: Beyond the n/2 Threshold: Quantum Query Complexity for Computing Hamming Weight and Symmetric Functions
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Recovering exact Hamming weight and computing any symmetric Boolean function takes at most n/2+O(n1/3) quantum queries with bounded error; explicit symmetric functions require n/2+Ω(n1/3) queries.

Grade 0.389 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Yuan Deng, Zihan Hao, Honghao Lin, Qipeng Liu, Vahab Mirrokni, Jianan Shao, David P. Woodruff

Figure

Schematic of the symmetric functions F2m,0 and F2m,R across input Hamming weights, highlighting the central zero-valued plateaus of width 2 and 2R+2 adjacent to alternating tail regions.

Asks

Is any additive overhead beyond n/2 unavoidable for quantum query algorithms computing a single Boolean output, and what is its optimal worst-case order?

Before

was n/2+O(n) queries for all Boolean functions via oracle interrogation (van Dam 1998)

But

Worst-case query complexity; bounded constant error; lower bound proven for symmetric Boolean functions.

Tools

quantum counting · Grover search · coherent quantum walk on matchings · one-query parity sampling

Abstract

The oracle-interrogation algorithm [van Dam, FOCS '98] computes every n-bit Boolean function with bounded error using n/2+O(√n) quantum queries. In contrast, parity can be computed exactly using lceiln/2rceil queries, but whether an additive overhead beyond n/2 is necessary for a single Boolean output has remained open. In this work, we construct an explicit family of symmetric Boolean functions requiring n/2+Ω(n^(1/3)) quantum queries at a fixed positive constant error. We also give an algorithm that recovers the exact Hamming weight using n/2+O(n^(1/3)) quantum queries with bounded error, and therefore computes every symmetric Boolean function within the same query bound. Together, these results determine the optimal additive order for Hamming weight recovery and for the worst case over symmetric Boolean functions at sufficiently small constant error.

item.title: pfoqcompiler: Efficient Compilation of Quantum Control in Recursive First-Order Quantum Programs
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Compiler pfoqcompiler merges compatible recursive calls across quantum branches in FOQ. Produces polynomial-size circuits for weakly well-founded bounded-width programs and polylogarithmic depth under weak recursive halving, removing asymptotic sequentialization overhead without exponential ancilla overhead.

Grade 0.370 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Mário Silva (LMF, QuaCS), Alexandre Guernut (MOCQUA), Marco Lewis (LMF, QuaCS)

Asks

Can recursive quantum control in first-order quantum languages be compiled into parallelized circuits without incurring exponential ancillary qubit overhead or exponential circuit depth?

Before

Naive compilation yields exponential circuit depth from sequentializing branches; standard parallelization techniques require an exponential number of ancillary qubits.

But

Applies to FOQ programs satisfying syntactically checkable weak well-foundedness, bounded width, and weak uniformity/halving conditions.

Tools

pfoqcompiler · first-order quantum language FOQ · syntactic analysis of recursive halving and uniformity · Qiskit backend

Abstract

Recursive quantum control allows for simple and concise descriptions of algorithms. However, a naive circuit compilation sequentializes the different branches of the quantum if-statement and results in an exponential increase in circuit depth. Existing techniques can parallelize these branches, but do so at the cost of an exponential number of ancillary qubits. We present pfoqcompiler, a compiler targeting Qiskit for the first-order quantum programming language FOQ that exploits program structure to merge compatible recursive procedure calls across quantum branches. We introduce weaker syntactically-checkable conditions for well-foundedness, recursive halving, and uniformity, while preserving previously demonstrated complexity characterizations. For weakly well-founded bounded-width programs, the compiler produces polynomial-size circuits; weakly recursively halving programs additionally yield polylogarithmic depth, while weak uniformity removes the asymptotic overhead of branch sequentialization.

item.title: Differentiable Digital Twins for Optimization, Calibration, and Characterization of Neutral-Atom- and Ion-based Quantum Computers
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Introduced differentiable-digital-twin software framework `qruise-toolset` for atomic qubits, simulating single-qubit randomized benchmarking with error per Clifford of 1.11(30)×10−3 and achieving quantum volume of 24=16 with 83.1% mean heavy-output probability.

Grade 0.359 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Marco Rossignolo, Lorena C. Bianchet, Anurag Saha Roy, Shai Machnes

Figure

Heavy-output probability per circuit for 200 random four-qubit square circuits of depth 4. The cumulative mean (solid line) stays at 83.1%, exceeding the 2/3 pass threshold (dashed line) to demonstrate a quantum volume of 16.

Asks

How can atomic quantum processor dynamics and hardware control stacks be modelled and calibrated using end-to-end automatic differentiation?

But

Demonstrated primarily in numerical simulation; subject to exponential resource scaling for full state and process tomography.

Tools

automatic differentiation · quantum optimal control · digital twin modeling · Qiskit backend emulation · randomized benchmarking

Abstract

Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.

item.title: Quantum subsets discrimination and key sifting with success probability one
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Decomposing input Gram matrices over unpredictable subset partitions yields error-free subset discrimination with success probability equal to 1, even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent states. For equidistant states, unit success holds when ⟨φi|φj⟩=(N−2)/(2N−2).

Grade 0.356 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing” · D. A. Kronberg

Asks

Can the success probability of error-free subset discrimination bypass standard limits and reach unity for non-orthogonal quantum states?

Before

Subset discrimination and unambiguous state discrimination for non-orthogonal states strictly had success probability strictly below one for any fixed partition.

But

Restricted to pure states. Yields an unpredictable subset partition rather than a preselected one. Lacks an explicit cost-effective optical implementation and full finite-error security proof for the derived QKD protocol.

Tools

Gram matrix convex decomposition · Kraus map · randomized positive operator-valued measure (POVM)

Abstract

Non-distinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states is the essential feature of quantum mechanics. In particular, one cannot deterministically orthogonalize the set of quantum states, while probabilistic orthogonalization is possible, including unambiguous state discrimination and discrimination between the subsets. Here, we propose a method for error-free subsets discrimination with significantly increased success probability, which may reach one even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent input states. This method may be applied in quantum cryptography: An alternative basis reconciliation procedure is described, which may provide unit sifting probability even for a large number of bases and for non-orthogonal states within each basis.

item.title: A Complete Calculus for Hamiltonian Quantum Programming
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Introduced Hamilton, a process calculus for Hamiltonian quantum computing. Semantics is fully abstract, equational theory is complete and decidable, and expressible Hamiltonians are precisely those with dyadic rational Pauli coefficients m/2k.

Grade 0.349 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian simulation algorithms: product formulas, qubitization, signal proce…” · Jacques Carette, Chris Heunen, Robin Kaarsgaard, Neil J. Ross, Amr Sabry

Figure

Survival probability |a3(t)|2 of a proton in a hydrogen bond at state |11⟩ over time t up to 40 fs. Refined compiled circuits at n=4 track the exact continuous Hamiltonian evolution with maximum deviation ≤0.0042.

Asks

Can quantum programming treat continuous Hamiltonian evolution as an additive concurrent primitive with a sound, complete, and fully abstract equational calculus?

Before

Circuit-level equational reasoning (like ZX phase gadgets or Πk) handles unitaries at fixed precision but lacks an equational theory complete for Hamiltonians and their additive combinations.

But

Only targets first-order Lie-Trotter splittings; circuit emissions lack multi-qubit resynthesis/optimization (e.g. 18 CNOTs per step instead of 3); purely unitary with no dissipative dynamics, mid-circuit measurement, or block encoding.

Tools

Lie-Trotter product formula · Π_k quantum circuit calculus · concurrent process algebra · Agda formal proof verification

Abstract

Given the forces acting on a quantum particle, a Hamiltonian models its continuous evolution. Quantum computers evolve Hamiltonians to simulate physical systems, to solve optimisation problems, and to estimate eigenvalues, and even the popular circuit abstraction is compiled to Hamiltonians on the hardware. We introduce Hamilton, a process calculus whose parallel operator is the sum of interactions acting simultaneously. Its operational semantics is the Lie-Trotter product formula, which recovers a sum as the limit of ever finer sequential interleavings; compiling a program means halving it to a chosen precision and unrolling the interleaving into a circuit. The semantics is fully abstract, the expressible Hamiltonians are exactly those whose Pauli coefficients have the form m/2^k, the precision that successive halving reaches, and the equational theory is complete and decidable. A full implementation compiles Hamilton programs to circuits and decides their equivalence, and Agda proofs sanity-check the core metatheory.
